interactions.label: A bullet recovered during post-mortem shows spiral groove marks on its surface.

params.question: A bullet recovered during post-mortem shows spiral groove marks on its surface. What does this finding indicate about the weapon used?

answers.text: The weapon was a shotgun with a smooth-bore barrel

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Smooth-bore barrels have no spiral grooves and are characteristic of shotguns. A shotgun fires pellets or slugs and does not leave rifling marks on projectiles.

answers.text: The weapon had a rifled barrel, and the marks can be matched to the specific firearm

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Spiral grooves in a rifled barrel spin the bullet for accuracy and impart unique marks. Since each weapon's rifling pattern is unique, forensic examiners can match the recovered bullet to the exact gun that fired it.

answers.text: The weapon was a manually repeating bolt-action rifle loaded with a slug

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While bolt-action rifles are rifled and do leave such marks, this answer is too specific about the mechanism. The groove marks tell you the barrel was rifled, not whether the action was bolt, lever, or semi-automatic.

answers.text: The marks are post-mortem artefacts from the bullet striking bone

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Spiral groove marks on a recovered bullet are produced by the rifling inside the barrel, not by contact with bone or tissue. They are consistent, reproducible, and form the basis of forensic ballistic identification.

overallFeedback.feedback: Rifled barrels have spiral grooves that spin the bullet for accuracy. These grooves leave marks unique to each weapon, allowing forensic matching of a recovered bullet to the exact firearm that fired it.
Well done. Rifling marks are like a weapon's fingerprint — unique to each firearm and invaluable in forensic identification.

interactions.label: A bullet's calibre is the most important factor determining the severity of tiss

params.question: A bullet's calibre is the most important factor determining the severity of tissue damage it causes.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Calibre is the internal diameter of the barrel and the bullet, but it does not determine lethality on its own. Kinetic energy scales with the square of velocity, so muzzle velocity matters far more than bullet diameter. A .22 calibre rifle bullet can be more lethal than a larger-calibre pistol bullet because of its much higher velocity.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Right. Calibre measures only the bullet's diameter, not its destructive potential. Kinetic energy — which scales with the square of velocity — is the principal driver of tissue damage. A small-calibre .22 rifle bullet at high muzzle velocity can cause more lethal injury than a larger-calibre pistol bullet at lower velocity.

params.question: A gunshot entrance wound shows tattooing (powder stippling) around the margins but no blackening, singeing, or sooting on the skin surface. What is the most likely range of fire?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In a contact wound, soot and gas are driven deep into the wound track, not deposited on the skin surface. You would also expect a cruciform tear if the muzzle was pressed against bone.
Close-range wounds show both blackening on the skin surface AND tattooing. The complete absence of blackening here rules out close range.

Correct. Unburnt powder particles travel farther than soot, so tattooing persists beyond the distance at which blackening disappears. Tattooing without blackening places the muzzle at approximately 15 to 60 cm from the target.
At distant range, even tattooing disappears. Only the abrasion collar around a clean, punched-out entrance wound remains as a diagnostic feature.

overallFeedback.feedback: Each combustion product settles at a characteristic distance: singeing and blackening appear at close range, tattooing persists to intermediate range, and only the abrasion collar remains at distant range. Tattooing WITHOUT blackening places the muzzle at approximately 15–60 cm.
Excellent. Combustion products vanish in a predictable sequence as range increases, and reading which features are present versus absent is how a forensic physician estimates the firing distance.

interactions.label: Which of the following wound descriptions would meet the standard required for a

params.question: Which of the following wound descriptions would meet the standard required for a medico-legal report on a gunshot injury?

answers.text: A circular wound with some blackening on the right side of the head

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This description is too vague for court use. It lacks precise measurements, exact anatomical location relative to bony landmarks, and specific characterisation of individual features such as the abrasion collar and the extent of blackening.

answers.text: A 9 mm circular, punched-out wound, 2 cm anterior to the right external auditory meatus, with a 2 mm abrasion collar and 4 cm radius of sooty blackening, no tattooing

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. This description specifies wound size, shape, exact location relative to a bony landmark, abrasion collar dimensions, blackening radius, and the absence of tattooing — precise enough that another physician could reconstruct the wound independently.

answers.text: A gunshot wound of entry on the right temple, consistent with close range

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While this includes a range opinion, it lacks the measurements and specific features that justify that opinion. A medico-legal report must present findings first, so any reader can independently verify the conclusion.

answers.text: A small round hole on the head with dark marks around it, likely caused by a firearm

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Terms like 'small,' 'dark marks,' and 'likely' are imprecise and subjective. A medico-legal report requires exact measurements in millimetres, standardised anatomical terms, and specific characterisation of each wound feature.

overallFeedback.feedback: A court-credible wound description must include exact size, shape, location relative to bony landmarks, abrasion collar dimensions, zone of blackening, tattooing, singeing, and foreign material — precise enough that another physician could reconstruct the wound from your description alone.
Well done. Precise, reproducible documentation is what makes a forensic wound report credible in court — every measurement and landmark you include strengthens the medico-legal opinion.
